course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
lesson.summary: How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.
learningGoals: Explain how the Revolution's ideals led some Americans to call for the abolition of slavery and greater political democracy.
Explain what republican motherhood was and why it gained popularity.
Describe the global impact of the American Revolution in France, Haiti, and Latin America.
lesson.bigIdea: The Revolution's ideals made inequalities in American society harder to ignore, but they were applied unevenly and left slavery and many exclusions in place.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain the various ways the Revolution affected society and to describe its global impact. Look for both the change that Revolutionary ideals produced and the limits on that change.

sections.title: Equality, slavery, and political democracy

blocks.text: During and after the American Revolution, an increased awareness of inequalities in society motivated some individuals and groups to call for the abolition of slavery and greater political democracy in the new state and national governments. Many Patriots saw a contradiction between demanding liberty from Britain and holding people in slavery. Quakers and other reformers led antislavery efforts, and enslaved and free Black Americans petitioned for freedom, used the courts, and some served in the Continental Army.

The result was uneven. Vermont's 1777 constitution banned slavery, Pennsylvania began gradual emancipation in 1780, and Massachusetts courts ended slavery in the state in the 1780s, while other northern states adopted gradual emancipation laws in the years that followed. Slavery remained central to the economy of the South. In 1775 Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, offered freedom to enslaved people who left rebel owners and joined the British, and thousands of enslaved people fled to British lines during the war.

Calls for greater political democracy also appeared in the new state governments. Some states widened participation, but property qualifications for voting remained common, and women and most free Black men could not vote in most states.

sections.takeaway: The Revolution encouraged antislavery action and wider political participation, but both advanced unevenly.

sections.title: Women and republican motherhood

blocks.text: Women contributed to the Revolutionary cause by boycotting British goods, running farms and businesses, raising money, nursing the wounded, and following the army. In response to women's participation in the American Revolution, Enlightenment ideas, and women's appeals for expanded roles, an ideal of “republican motherhood” gained popularity. It called on women to teach republican values within the family and granted women a new importance in American political culture.

Abigail Adams, writing to her husband John Adams while he served in Congress in 1776, urged him to consider women's legal position as the new government was shaped. The ideal of republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role and encouraged the education of girls, but it did not give women the vote or equal legal rights.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Republican motherhood expanded women's civic importance without giving women political rights. It placed women's political role within the home.

sections.takeaway: Republican motherhood gave women a civic role as teachers of republican values, without political equality.

sections.title: The global impact of the Revolution
sections.conceptTitle: The global impact of the Revolution

blocks.text: The American Revolution and the ideals set forth in the Declaration of Independence reverberated in France, Haiti, and Latin America, inspiring future independence movements. In France, the American example and ideas about natural rights and popular government helped inspire revolutionaries in 1789. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, an uprising by enslaved people that began in 1791 led to the independent Republic of Haiti in 1804. In the early 1800s, independence movements spread across Spanish and Portuguese America.
Each of these movements had its own causes and its own leaders, so the American Revolution is best seen as one important influence among several.

sections.takeaway: The Revolution's ideals helped inspire later independence movements in France, Haiti, and Latin America.

connections.title: Writing new governments
connections.body: Revolutionary ideals shaped the constitutions that the states wrote and the national government they created. Topic 3.7 follows those experiments.
connections.transferQuestion: Why did the Revolution's ideals of equality lead to emancipation in some states but not others?
connections.feedback: A strong answer connects the economic importance of slavery to the differences between northern and southern states.
